actions.name: Mental status exam - appearance and behavior
actions.result: Patient observed pacing continuously during video call, shifting weight foot to foot, unable to remain seated for more than ~30 seconds. Dressed appropriately, fair hygiene. Appears restless and uncomfortable.

actions.name: Mood and affect assessment
actions.result: Mood described by patient as 'on edge, tired.' Affect restricted but reactive; some irritability noted when discussing hospitalization. No euphoria or elation observed.

actions.name: Thought process and content assessment
actions.result: Thought process linear and goal-directed. Reports residual auditory hallucinations (voices commenting on him) occurring in evenings, now described as 'quieter' than during admission. No delusional content elicited today. Insight into illness partial.

actions.name: Suicide and homicide risk assessment
actions.result: Patient denies current or recent suicidal ideation, intent, or plan. Denies homicidal ideation or intent to harm others. No access to firearms reported. States voices do not command him to hurt himself or others.

actions.name: Extrapyramidal symptom screen (self/camera-guided)
actions.result: Patient reports inner restlessness and inability to sit still (consistent with akathisia). On camera-guided exam: mild cogwheel-type stiffness reported by patient in arms, no visible tremor at rest, no dystonia or oculogyric crisis observed. Gait steady but patient paces rather than walks purposefully.

actions.name: Sleep pattern assessment
actions.result: Patient reports sleeping approximately 10 hours per night, feels groggy on waking. No early morning awakening or insomnia reported.

actions.name: Home blood pressure and pulse (patient-reported from home cuff)
actions.result: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, measured sitting, taken this morning per patient report.

actions.name: Weight check (patient-reported from home scale)
actions.result: Weight 172 lb, patient reports this is about 3 lb above pre-admission weight.

actions.name: Review discharge medication reconciliation
actions.result: Discharge prescription: Risperidone 4 mg PO nightly, quantity 14 tablets (14-day supply), 0 refills, with instruction to follow up with outpatient psychiatry within 7-10 days.

actions.name: Review pharmacy fill history
actions.result: Pharmacy record shows the discharge risperidone prescription was filled once, for 7 tablets, 8 days ago. No subsequent fills or refill requests on file.

actions.name: Review outpatient psychiatry follow-up appointment status
actions.result: No outpatient psychiatry follow-up appointment is documented as scheduled or completed since discharge 8 days ago.

actions.name: Review discharge summary diagnosis and plan
actions.result: Discharge diagnosis: First episode psychosis, unspecified. Hospital course: two-week inpatient admission, started risperidone 4 mg nightly, discharged with instructions for outpatient psychiatry follow-up and this nursing check-in call.

actions.name: PHQ-9 depression screen (administered verbally)
actions.result: Score 6/27 (mild range). Positive items: trouble sleeping, feeling tired, trouble concentrating. Denies anhedonia at a level suggesting major depression. No item endorsed for thoughts of self-harm.

actions.name: Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) screening
actions.result: Screens negative for suicidal ideation, lifetime or current. No history of suicidal behavior or self-harm reported.

actions.name: Review substance use documentation from admission
actions.result: Admission note documents patient reports prior intermittent cannabis use (several times per month) in the year preceding admission; no documented stimulant, opioid, or hallucinogen use.

actions.name: Orientation and cognition check
actions.result: Patient alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Able to recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. Attention intact to serial tasks.

artifacts.title: Inpatient Discharge Summary
artifacts.author: Inpatient Psychiatry Attending
artifacts.body: 24-year-old male admitted for a first episode of psychosis with auditory hallucinations and disorganized behavior over approximately 3 weeks prior to admission, per family (grandmother) report. No prior psychiatric hospitalizations. Started risperidone, titrated to 4 mg nightly with good tolerance of acute agitation; some early reports of restlessness noted by nursing staff on the unit, which the patient attributed to 'nerves.' Admission substance use history: cannabis use several times monthly over the past year, no other substances reported or detected on urine toxicology at admission. Diagnosis: First episode psychosis, unspecified (rule out schizophreniform disorder, further workup to be completed outpatient). Discharged home with grandmother, who was present for discharge teaching. Plan: outpatient psychiatry follow-up within 7-10 days, nursing check-in call scheduled day 7-8 post-discharge, continue risperidone 4 mg nightly, follow up on EPS/akathisia symptoms, monitor for medication adherence and substance use.

artifacts.title: Pharmacy Fill History
artifacts.author: Community Pharmacy (electronic record)
artifacts.body: Risperidone 4 mg tablets, prescribed quantity 14, 0 refills authorized. Fill #1: filled 8 days ago, quantity dispensed 7 tablets (patient requested partial fill, stated cost concern at time of pick-up). No fill #2 on record. No refill requests received by pharmacy since.

facts.says: It started maybe like 2 or 3 days after they started the medicine in the hospital, and it's still here.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he has been taking risperidone every night as prescribed.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy fill history shows only one partial fill of 7 tablets 8 days ago with no refills, and patient later discloses skipping the last 3 nights; a 7-tablet fill 8 days ago cannot cover 8 nights of nightly dosing through today.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Always verify stated adherence against objective sources (pharmacy fill data, pill counts) rather than accepting self-report alone, especially when side effects create incentive to underreport nonadherence; approach discrepancies with curiosity, not confrontation.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports the voices are 'quieter' and implies they are nearly resolved.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Self-rated voice intensity trend chart shows a plateau at 4/10 from day 7 to day 8 rather than continued improvement, suggesting symptom control may be stalling, possibly related to missed doses.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Trend data can reveal plateauing or subtle worsening that a single reassuring statement from the patient may obscure; correlate symptom trends with adherence gaps before assuming steady improvement.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Medication-induced akathisia from risperidone 4 mg nightly, compounded by covert medication nonadherence (missed last 3 nights, only partial pharmacy fill obtained) and residual, improving but persistent auditory hallucinations in a patient 8 days post-discharge from first-episode psychosis admission, with an overdue outpatient psychiatry follow-up and recent cannabis use.
differential: Akathisia (extrapyramidal side effect of risperidone) - most consistent with description of inner restlessness, pacing, onset days after starting medication
Psychotic relapse/worsening agitation - less likely given linear thought process, improving (not worsening) hallucination trend, and clear temporal link of restlessness to medication start
Generalized anxiety related to fear of rehospitalization and stigma - contributing but not primary driver of motor restlessness
Cannabis-induced anxiety/restlessness - possible contributor but restlessness predates and is distinct in character from reported cannabis effects
Caffeine-related jitteriness - unlikely given stable, modest caffeine intake (distractor)
keyFindings: Continuous pacing and inability to sit still observed on camera, consistent with akathisia, onset 2-3 days after starting risperidone in hospital
Subjective arm stiffness without tremor; sleeping 10 hours but waking groggy
Patient states full adherence, but pharmacy fill history shows only one 7-tablet partial fill 8 days ago and patient later discloses skipping last 3 nights
Residual evening auditory hallucinations (non-command, commenting type), self-rated intensity plateaued at 4/10 over the last 2 days rather than continuing to improve
C-SSRS and direct questioning negative for suicidal or homicidal ideation, no command hallucinations to harm self/others
Cannabis use twice this week, used by patient to self-manage restlessness
No outpatient psychiatry follow-up appointment scheduled or completed since discharge 8 days ago, despite referral faxed at discharge
Significant fear of rehospitalization and stigma at college underlying guardedness and nonadherence
plan: Complete and document full mental status exam, EPS/akathisia screen, and suicide/homicide risk assessment (C-SSRS) this visit

Communicate urgently with prescribing/outpatient psychiatry (or on-call psychiatric provider) regarding significant akathisia and partial medication nonadherence so dose or agent can be reassessed by the prescriber - this is outside independent nursing scope to adjust
Facilitate active scheduling of overdue outpatient psychiatry follow-up; consider warm handoff/same-week urgent appointment given medication intolerance and partial adherence

Provide psychoeducation: akathisia is a treatable medication side effect, not a sign the medication is 'poisoning' him or that he is getting worse; encourage not stopping medication abruptly without provider guidance, and report side effects promptly
Discuss cannabis use and psychosis risk in a nonjudgmental, harm-reduction-oriented way; recommend reducing use and discuss with psychiatry
Address cost/access barrier to the full prescription fill; connect with pharmacy assistance program or social work/case management
Support disclosure to grandmother and care team with patient's consent to strengthen home support and medication monitoring
Reassure regarding confidentiality at college per policy while clarifying nurse's duty to escalate safety concerns if they arise
Schedule close follow-up contact (e.g., 24-48 hour check-in call) given medication intolerance and adherence gap, pending psychiatry input
Document SBAR summary and risk assessment clearly, including the adherence/pharmacy discrepancy and plan for provider notification
redFlags: Partial medication adherence in a patient with first-episode psychosis significantly raises relapse risk and should prompt urgent provider communication
Any emergence of command hallucinations to harm self or others, or any suicidal/homicidal ideation, would require immediate escalation and possibly emergency evaluation
Worsening (rather than plateauing) auditory hallucinations or new disorganized behavior would be a red flag for relapse

Severe, worsening akathisia carries a small but documented association with increased agitation, distress, and suicidality risk and must be reported promptly, not managed by stopping medication abruptly without guidance
Missed outpatient psychiatry follow-up beyond the recommended window needs active remediation, not passive tracking
educationPoints: Akathisia is a common, uncomfortable extrapyramidal side effect of antipsychotics like risperidone that can mimic anxiety or agitation but has a distinct inner restlessness quality and clear temporal link to medication start/dose changes

Self-reported adherence is often inaccurate, especially when side effects are distressing; objective data (pharmacy fill records, pill counts) should be reviewed and discrepancies explored with curiosity rather than confrontation
Abruptly stopping antipsychotics without provider guidance can increase relapse risk even when the motivation (intolerable side effects) is understandable
Cannabis use can worsen psychotic symptoms over time and interact with antipsychotic efficacy; harm-reduction conversations are more effective than confrontation
Fear of rehospitalization and stigma can drive nondisclosure; establishing trust and clarifying the goal of keeping the patient safely out of the hospital can improve honesty and engagement
Trend data (e.g., symptom rating charts) should be reviewed over time rather than relying on a single reassuring verbal report, since plateaus or subtle worsening can be missed
Nursing scope includes thorough assessment, psychoeducation, risk screening, and escalation/communication with prescribers - not independent medication changes

patient.name: Devon Clarke
patient.appearance: A young man of average build with short dark hair, wearing a plain T-shirt, appears tired with slightly flushed cheeks. He is visibly unable to stay seated, frequently standing up, pacing across the frame of the camera, and shifting his weight from foot to foot throughout the call. His bedroom is dimly lit with posters on the wall; he glances at the door occasionally as if checking who might overhear.

persona.personality: Guarded and anxious at first, but earnest and cooperative once he feels safe; has a dry, understated sense of humor that surfaces when he relaxes.
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks in short, hedging sentences when nervous; opens up with more detail and emotion once trust is established; avoids clinical jargon, uses his own descriptive phrases.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious, physically agitated, fearful of being judged or sent back to the hospital, underlying hope that he can return to normal life.
persona.background: Grew up in the Bronx after his family moved from Jamaica when he was a child; lives with his grandmother, who raised him and has been his main support since his hospitalization. He is enrolled part-time at a community college studying business, works occasionally helping a cousin with deliveries, and had never experienced any mental health issues before this first episode.
speechExamples: I've just been really restless, like I have to keep moving all the time.
Please don't send me back to the hospital. I just got out, I can't go through that again.
Okay, honestly... I haven't taken it the last three nights.
Nobody at my school knows I was in the hospital. I really don't want that getting out.
I just want to be able to sit in class again without feeling like I'm going to jump out of my skin.
concerns: Fear of being readmitted to the hospital if he admits his symptoms are not fully controlled
Worry that classmates or professors at college will find out about his hospitalization
Confusion and fear about what a 'psychosis' diagnosis means for his future
Frustration that the medication meant to help him is causing unbearable restlessness
Concern about disappointing or worrying his grandmother

scenario.studentBrief: You are a psychiatric-mental health nursing student conducting a telehealth post-discharge check-in with Devon Clarke, a 24-year-old man who was discharged 8 days ago after a two-week inpatient admission for a first episode of psychosis. He was started on risperidone 4 mg nightly at discharge. This is a scheduled nursing follow-up call to assess his mental status, safety, and medication tolerance/adherence, and to coordinate ongoing care. You do not yet know his current symptom status, side effects, or adherence - assess thoroughly and build rapport before probing sensitive topics.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Restlessness and inability to sit still since starting antipsychotic medication after recent psychiatric hospitalization
scenario.openingLine: Hi... yeah, I've just been really restless, like I have to keep moving all the time. I can't even sit through my classes.
tasks: Perform a mental status exam including appearance, mood, affect, thought process, and perceptual disturbances via video
Conduct a thorough suicide/homicide risk assessment and screen for command hallucinations
Assess for extrapyramidal symptoms/akathisia and explore the timeline relative to medication start
Explore medication adherence sensitively, cross-check with pharmacy/record data, and identify any discrepancies
Screen for substance use and its relationship to symptoms
Provide psychoeducation and determine appropriate escalation/follow-up plan within nursing scope

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in his bedroom in the Bronx, New York, on his personal laptop
profile.summary: An 8-day post-discharge telehealth check-in with a 24-year-old man after a first psychotic episode, presenting with akathisia from risperidone that he has misattributed as the medication 'making him worse,' leading to covert nonadherence and a cost-related partial pharmacy fill, alongside residual but improving auditory hallucinations and recent cannabis use. The case teaches risk assessment, EPS recognition, rapport-based elicitation of hidden nonadherence/substance use, and appropriate nursing-scope escalation when outpatient follow-up has lapsed.
profile.title: Akathisia and Covert Nonadherence After First-Episode Psychosis Discharge
